newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak rates jump on fears of liquidity crunch.
newsitem.headline: Slovak rates jump on fears of liquidity crunch.

text.p: Slovak interbank rates on Tuesday jumped to over 30 percent on fears that the local money market was toward another liquidity shortage, dealers said.
They said one-day funds remain the most traded maturity, with rates at around 31 percent, up from 28 percent on Monday.

"I would say that it was a psychological effect that the state bond auction will drain more funds and even further shorten the market which drove the rates up," said Martin Hrozany, chief dealer at Credit Lyonnais.
The Finance Ministry earlier on Tuesday sold one-year state bonds worth 2.4 billion crowns at an average yield of 16.812 percent.
"But the high accepted yield show the ministry really needed the money and that they will spend it immediately, which means these funds will soon end up back in the banking sector," Hrozany added.
Traders said local banks now tend to attempt to meet their minimum reserves requirements (PMR) on a daily basis to avoid borrowing expensive funds at the end of each period.

"The sector is getting close to meeting PMR on 100 percent, but banks keep the funds to ensure they meet their PMR, which means that not much money is circulating on the market at the moment," said one local trader.
According to NBS figures, the banking sector lacked some 1.87 percent of funds needed to meet PMR later this month.

Traders said that even a meeting between the eight largest market players -- known as reference banks -- later on Tuesday was not expected to bring much positive news in solving the current market liquidity problems over longer term.

Some traders said earlier this week that the meeting could re-introduce an obligation to quote both bids and offers on certain volumes and maturities, an agreement which was valid before attack on the Slovak crown some two months ago.
"Market sentiment is that no such agreement will be made today, which means that we should not expect any radical improvement in trading activity in the near future," a foreign bank trader said.
